summary.text: 名 is traditionally explained as 夕, evening, together with 口, a speaking mouth: people call out their names when they cannot see one another. This is a received account of the graph, not a securely established explanation of its original motivation.

formation.text: The received analysis is semantic: 夕 sets an evening scene and 口 depicts speaking. A secondary proposal treats 夕 as a sound indicator, but the cited material does not establish that role; the graph’s original motivation remains uncertain.

components.text: 夕 is the upper element. Its basic sense is the time around sunset and moonrise, sometimes extending to night. In the received explanation of 名, it supplies the evening setting. 夕 and 月 once shared a moon-like form; later, a dot distinguished 月.

口 is the lower element. In the received explanation, it depicts the mouth used to speak one’s name. The cited accounts identify it in 名 but do not describe a separate graphic history for it within this character.

history.text: 名 is recorded in oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript, small-seal, and Shuowen forms. The selected oracle-style and Western Zhou bronze-style images are modern vector drawings of forms associated with 名; they show different examples, not a proven sequence of graphic change.

The night-identification account appears in the Shuowen explanation and is repeated in later descriptions. A competing proposal says 口 may once have written both 口 and 名, with 夕 added as a sound indicator associated with a graph later written 明. This proposal remains unverified, and the cited reconstructions do not support 夕 as a phonetic for 名.
A rare added-stroke form found on a stele is described as an unusual variant resembling an error, not as an ancestral form.

uncertainties.text: The traditional explanation relates the graph to 夕 and 口, but does not independently establish the original motivation. The proposed phonetic role for 夕 and its suggested connection with a graph later written 明 remain unverified.
The earliest cited oracle-bone token occurs in a place name; its date and interpretation are unresolved, and it is not an unambiguous ordinary use meaning “name.”
The cited uses and dictionary senses do not establish when personal-name, naming, inscription, reputation, or status meanings first arose, or a continuous path among them.

senses.text: The earliest cited use is a token in a place name; its precise interpretation is unresolved.

senses.period: Western Zhou bronze and Warring States manuscripts
senses.text: A Western Zhou inscription uses 名 as a verb meaning “name” or “designate”; Warring States manuscripts also attest name or designation uses. These examples do not establish when the sense first arose.
One bronze use is glossed as 銘, “inscription.” The evidence does not resolve whether this is a meaning development or 名 used to write a related word.
名 is used for a person’s name, though the cited material does not date the first occurrence of this sense.
名 also means to name or designate; the evidence does not establish its chronology relative to the noun sense.
Dictionary sources list reputation and status-related meanings, but do not establish when they arose or how they developed.

limitations.text: The earliest cited token is a place name, not an unambiguous use for an ordinary personal name. The available examples do not establish first dates or semantic links among the other senses.
The bronze use glossed as 銘 does not establish a development from “name” to “inscription”; it may represent 名 used to write a related word, but the relationship is unresolved.

evidence.text: A name called out 口 to hail someone at night 夕
Traditionally explained as identifying youself at night (夕) by saying (口) your name (名) because is too dark for others to see you.
自命也。从口从夕。夕者，冥也。冥不相見，故以口自名。

Ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意): 夕 (“crescent moon”) + 口 (“mouth”) — to say one's own name to identify oneself in the dark.
An alternative theory has been proposed based on Shang era texts. 口 was originally used to write both 口 and 名. 夕 standing for what later came to be written 明, was added as a phonetic indicator to disambiguate the two meanings.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *r-meŋ (“name”). Cognate with Tibetan མིང (ming), Burmese အမည် (a.many), and Mizo hming.

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Ancient Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: character evolution; graph structure and interpretation
evidence.text: The database lists 名 across oracle-bone, bronze (including inscription collection no. 04293), Chu manuscript, small-seal, and Shuowen stages. It describes the upper part as 夕 and lower as 口, and presents the traditional account that both are semantic: people unable to see one another at night speak their names to identify themselves. This supports the form sequence and records the received interpretation; it does not independently establish that interpretation as the original motivation.
evidence.title: 漢字「名」：字形演變

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: oracle-bone / bronze interpretation and attested uses
evidence.text: The database repeats the Shuowen night-identification account, then distinguishes uses: oracle-bone record 《乙》3290 has 名 in a place name; the Western Zhou 少虡 sword inscription has 名 as a verb ‘name/designate’ (朕余名之，謂之少虡); the bronze 鑄公華鐘 use is glossed as 銘 ‘inscription’. It also cites Warring States manuscript examples for ‘name/designation’, including 清華簡《楚居》簡9, 郭店簡《老子甲》簡18, and 郭店簡《太一生水》簡10. These examples show graph usage but do not, by themselves, establish a linear semantic chronology from the oracle-bone place name to later common-noun uses.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 夕 (includes 名 entry)

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Ancient Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database says 夕 and 月 originally both used a moon-like shape without a distinguishing dot; later graphic differentiation assigned the dotted shape to 月 and the undotted shape to 夕. It describes 夕’s basic sense as the time around sunset and moonrise, while noting that some usage extends to night. This makes the Shuowen explanation of 夕 as ‘darkness’ a historical gloss, not proof that night identification was the original formation mechanism of 名.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 夕

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: Shuowen account; senses; graphic variant note
evidence.text: The dictionary records the Shuowen explanation: 名 ‘self-designate’, from 口 and 夕, with 夕 glossed as darkness and the whole graph explained as speaking one’s name when people cannot see one another. Its listed senses include a person’s designation/name, naming, object names, written characters, conceptual names, status, reputation, fame, category, and classifier uses. It cites Cao Quan stele evidence for a rare altered graph form; the entry characterizes that form as an unusual added-stroke stele variant resembling an error, rather than evidence for an early ancestral shape.
evidence.title: A00508 名 — Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: Wiktionary Chinese character entry; reconstruction fields attributed there to Baxter–Sagart 2014 and Zhengzhang
evidence.field: historical pronunciation comparison; reconstruction system and scope
evidence.text: The page gives modern Beijing Mandarin míng for 名, Middle Chinese mjieng, Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *C.meŋ, and Zhengzhang Old Chinese *meŋ. The phonological similarity of reconstructed 名 and Mandarin míng is compatible with comparison of readings, but this evidence does not establish a phonetic role for 夕. The cited entry labels 名 itself as its Zhengzhang phonetic series; it does not provide a paired reconstruction showing 夕 as the phonetic in 名.

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

search_audit.outcome: Search found accessible character databases and variant dictionary. Inspected Sinica, CUHK, and Taiwan MOE character-specific pages. They support the traditional graphic account and cite inscriptional/manuscript uses; they do not establish original motivation independently.

search_audit.outcome: Search did not locate a primary study specifically adjudicating 名’s phonetic-vs-semantic analysis. General phonetic-character articles were not treated as evidence about 名.

search_audit.query: 名 earliest attestation oracle bone meaning name bronze inscriptions
search_audit.outcome: CUHK page inspected and reports oracle-bone place-name use, a Western Zhou bronze naming use, another bronze inscription use glossed 銘, and Warring States manuscript examples.

search_audit.query: Wiktionary 名 Baxter Sagart *C.meŋ Old Chinese 夕 phonetic
search_audit.outcome: Inspected the Chinese Wiktionary 名 page for multiple reconstruction systems and the alternative analysis. Local Baxter–Sagart TSV rows for 名, 夕, and 口 were cross-checked; 名 matches the page, while 夕 and 名 are phonetically dissimilar in that system.

search_audit.outcome: Results repeated the conventional analysis and secondary alternative; no primary paleographic defense of a 夕 phonetic component found.

search_audit.outcome: Secondary entry states the alternative; other results concern general orthographic or phonetic issues, not a direct analysis of 名. Treat the alternative as unverified.

gaps: The proposed alternative that 夕 functions as a phonetic indicator in 名 has not been supported here by a directly inspected primary paleographic study or a clear early inscriptional argument; its relationship to the claim that 口 originally wrote both words remains uncertain.

The earliest cited oracle-bone example is a place-name token, not an unambiguous ordinary common-noun ‘name’; the date and semantic interpretation of that token are not independently resolved in the inspected record.

The cited attestation sequence demonstrates varied uses but does not establish when ‘personal name’, ‘to name’, ‘reputation’, ‘rank/title’, or classifier senses first arose, nor a continuous semantic path between them. Dictionary sense order is not treated as chronology.
No visually inspected glyph facsimile was obtained in this research; database stage labels and cited catalog numbers are reported without claiming direct image examination.

Official Unicode Unihan character-specific pages for 名, 夕, and 口 could not be opened through the web tool. Local current-reading rows are noted, but their external click-through verification remains incomplete.
The Wiktionary proto-Sino-Tibetan cognacy suggestions were not independently investigated in this bounded search; no cognate claim is advanced here.
The proposal that 夕 stood for a graph later written 明 is not independently established in the inspected primary sources; it is retained only as an attributed secondary proposal.
The retrieved material repeats the traditional semantic 夕 + 口 explanation but does not independently demonstrate that it was the original motivation of the graph.

An alternative reported in the dossier—that 夕 served as a phonetic indicator, possibly associated with a graph later written 明—remains without a directly inspected primary paleographic defense here; it is not adopted as established analysis.
The earliest reported oracle-bone use is a place-name token, not an unambiguous common-noun ‘name’; the cited database page does not resolve its date or semantics further.

Attestations show place-name, naming, inscription, and Warring States name/designation uses, but they do not establish first dates for ‘personal name’, ‘reputation’, ‘rank’, classifier or other extensions, nor a continuous semantic path. Dictionary gloss order is not chronology.
No independent original-object/name borrowing analysis was needed for this graph account; no borrowing claim is advanced.

Modern readings and historical reconstruction comparisons are not reasserted as sound-component evidence. The local Mandarin rows for 名, 夕, and 口 lack verified official Unicode character-page click-throughs in this invocation; Unihan is current metadata and would not itself establish an ancient sound relationship.
The official Xiaoxuetang CC0 terms were inspected, but its character-specific query did not load through the web tool, so no source-label-specific glyph could be selected.

Commons vector glyphs are modern redrawings rather than artifact photographs. Their exact original-file pages were verified, but browser fetches of both SVG assets failed with cache misses; pixels were not visually inspected.

items.period: Shang oracle-bone script style; the file page does not provide a narrower date for this character image
items.caption: A modern vector rendering of 名 in Shang oracle-bone script style, catalogued as J02120. The image shows a small mouth-like form beside a larger curved form; it is a drawing, not an artifact photograph.
items.alt: Black oracle-script drawing with a small rounded, open form on the left and a tall curved form on the right.
items.selection_reason: This character-specific early-script drawing helps readers see a form associated with 名. The received interpretation connects 口 and 夕 with calling one’s name in darkness, though the evidence does not establish that account as the graph’s original motivation.
items.rights: Public domain release stated on the file page.

items.period: Western Zhou bronze-script style; cited as B01197 and 南宮乎鐘, 集成00181
items.tradition: Western Zhou bronze script, modern vector redraw
items.caption: A modern vector rendering of 名 in Western Zhou bronze-script style, catalogued as B01197 and associated with the 南宮乎鐘 inscription. It is a drawing of a form, not a vessel photograph.
items.alt: Black bronze-script drawing with a broad, curved upper form containing an opening and a separate lower curved form.
items.selection_reason: This character-specific bronze-script drawing provides another attested inscriptional form for comparison. It complements the oracle-style rendering without implying a direct sequence of graphic change.
items.rights: Public domain release stated on the file page.

limitations.text: Both images are modern vector redrawings rather than photographs of original inscriptions. The traditional account relates 名 to 口 and 夕 and to identifying oneself by speaking in darkness, but it is not independently established here as the graph’s original motivation.
